title: Strokes you can type
goal: Some chords are physically impossible. The dictionary never writes one, and a stroke that misses is still read back sensibly.

blocks.x: What the right pinky can't do
The right pinky has four keys in a block:

items: It can press **one** key, **two in a line** ([[-TS]], [[-DZ]], [[-TD]], [[-SZ]]), or **all four**.
It cannot press a **diagonal pair** (`-TZ`, `-SD`) or **exactly three**.
This is a limit of the hand, found by typing *cadence* as `KAEUPBSD`. So no outline contains such a chord.
**Swap**, still one stroke: the voiced and unvoiced partner trade places. [[cadence|KAEUPBTS]], [[utters|URTS]], [[silenced|SAOEUPBLTS]].
**Split**, two strokes, if no swap is free: the pinky keys that fit stay, the rest go to a joined stroke. `-SD` becomes `-S` then `+-D`.
A few rare words have no outline at all because their only repair would change a sound. The fallback reads their strokes.

blocks.x: You never decide this. If a word's outline looks different from the sounds, this is usually why.
A stroke the dictionary does not have is read back into sounds, as a last resort, by the same tables you learned in lessons 3 to 6.

items: **A stroke with no vowel invents none.** `-T` alone reads as *t*.
**A suffix chord always reads as the suffix.** `STKPW/+-D` is *zed*, not *zd*.
**A first stroke that is already a word reads as that word.** `SKP` is a brief for *and*; `SKP/+-R` reads *ander*, not gibberish.

blocks.x: So an almost-right outline still lands near the word you meant. Your typing never produces a hole.

blocks.q: Which of these can the right pinky press?
blocks.why: `-D` over `-Z` are in the same column, a line. The other two are diagonals.
